entities.name: Umayyad Caliphate
entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
The Umayyad Caliphate (Arabic: الخلافة الأموية, al-Khilāfa al-Umawīya) — established in 661 CE when Muawiyah ibn Abi Sufyan became caliph following Ali's assassination, ruled from Damascus until 750 CE — was the Islamic world's first hereditary dynasty, expanding Islam from Spain and Portugal in the west to Central Asia and the borders of India and China in the east, creating one of the largest empires in history and spreading Islam across a vast territory that still has Muslim majorities today.

The Umayyad expansion was extraordinary: within 90 years of Muhammad's death, the Islamic world stretched from the Iberian Peninsula (Al-Andalus, conquered 711-718 CE) to the Indus Valley (Sindh conquered 711-712 CE) and Central Asia (Transoxiana, 705-715 CE). The Battle of Poitiers/Tours (732 CE) in France — where Charles Martel defeated the Umayyad forces — is often cited as the limit of westward Islamic expansion in Europe, though the significance of this single battle is debated by historians.

The Umayyad period established several enduring features of Islamic civilization: Arabic as the administrative and cultural language across the empire (replacing Greek, Persian, and Coptic in administration), the gold dinar and silver dirham as the Islamic monetary standard, the construction of iconic early Islamic monuments (the Dome of the Rock in Jerusalem, 691 CE; the Great Mosque of Damascus, 706-714 CE), and the first systematic translation movement of Greek scientific texts into Arabic. The Umayyad Caliphate's overthrow by the Abbasids in 750 CE (one surviving branch established the Emirate of Córdoba in Spain) ended the Umayyad dynasty's rule.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: The Umayyad Caliphate — expanding Islam from Spain to Central Asia, building the Dome of the Rock, establishing Arabic as the imperial language — is one of history's most consequential empires whose territorial expansion spread Islam across territories with Muslim majorities today.
